To ford something means to cross a body of water — a river, stream, or creek — by walking, riding, or driving through it, rather than using a bridge or a boat.
The one thing that makes "ford" special

When you ford water, you go directly through it. The water is shallow enough that you can physically pass through it and come out the other side. This is what separates "ford" from simply "cross." You can cross a river by bridge, by boat, by swimming — but you ford it only when you are literally moving through the water itself, with your feet (or wheels) touching the bottom.

You can only ford water that is shallow enough to pass through safely. A deep, rushing river cannot be forded — it must be bridged or boated. Fordin happens at the shallowest and calmest section of a body of water, where the depth is low enough and the current manageable enough to walk or drive through. Think knee-deep or waist-deep at most for a person on foot.
Who does the fordin — and what they ford

• People on foot ford streams and shallow rivers, often as part of hiking or military campaigns. "The soldiers forded the river before dawn."
  • People on horseback have historically forded rivers, since a horse can wade through water that would stop a cart or foot soldier. "The cavalry forded the creek with ease."
  • Vehicles — especially off-road ones — ford water too. Jeeps, military trucks, and four-wheel-drive vehicles are often described by their ability to ford a certain depth of water. "This SUV can ford up to 60 centimetres of water."

• "We forded three streams before reaching the campsite." — The hikers walked through three shallow streams along the way.
  • "The explorers had to ford the swollen river at its narrowest point." — They crossed it by wading through, finding where it was least dangerous.
  • "Can this jeep ford that creek?" — Is the jeep capable of driving through the creek?
  • "They forded the river under heavy fire." — A military scenario where troops crossed through the water.

"Ford" is almost entirely a literal word. It is not commonly used in a figurative sense (unlike words such as "navigate" or "wade through," which are often used to describe abstract challenges like "navigating a difficult situation"). If someone says "we had to ford many obstacles," it would sound unusual and poetic at best. Stick to using "ford" for actual water.

• It does not mean to swim across. Swimming implies the water is deep; fordin implies it is shallow enough to walk or drive through with your feet on the bottom.
  • It does not mean to cross by bridge or boat. Those methods keep you out of the water; fordin puts you in it.
  • It does not mean to cross any kind of terrain — only bodies of water.
The full picture in one sentence
To ford is to cross a body of water by moving directly through its shallows — on foot, horseback, or in a vehicle — without a bridge or boat.
